questions.q: About how far from Earth is the EPIC camera?
questions.do: Read the first row, Camera's distance from Earth, in the Checks table.
questions.a: About 1.5 million km, near the L1 balance point between Earth and the Sun. DSCOVR loops around L1 rather than sitting exactly on it.

questions.q: How far does the centre of the picture move each hour, and in which direction? If one picture is centred at 80°E, where is a picture taken 2 hours later centred?
questions.do: Press Spin the day and watch Directly under the camera change. Read the How fast the view turns row in the Checks table and the text in How to read the pictures.
questions.a: About 15° west every hour, because Earth turns once in 24 hours (360° ÷ 24 = 15°). Two hours later the centre is about 80° − 30° = 50°E.

questions.q: How long does light take to travel from Earth to the camera?
questions.do: Read Camera's distance from Earth and Light from Earth to camera in the details box. Check the rule with the numbers.
questions.a: About 5 seconds. Time = distance ÷ speed of light. For 1,500,000 km: 1,500,000 ÷ 299,792 km/s ≈ 5.0 s.

questions.q: Why does every EPIC photograph show a fully lit Earth, never a half-lit one?
questions.do: Read Angle between camera and Sun, seen from Earth in the details box and look at the Where the camera is map.
questions.a: DSCOVR sits almost on the line from Earth to the Sun, so the angle is small. The camera looks at Earth from nearly the Sun's direction, so it sees the whole sunlit face.

questions.q: The first photograph of the whole round Earth was taken in 1972. Who took it, and how is today’s picture different?
questions.do: Read the introduction at the top of the page, then press Spin the day.
questions.a: The Apollo 17 crew took the “Blue Marble” on 7 December 1972, on their way to the Moon: a single snapshot. Since 2015 the EPIC camera on DSCOVR has photographed the whole sunlit Earth about a dozen times every day, so you can watch a full day turn.
